Dear Federal Investigators, Nonprofit Advocates, Media, & Oversight Officials,

We are releasing a new open-source tool: the NPI Non-Profiteer Index Calculator — a free, auditable software platform designed to identify tax fraud, credential harvesting, and trafficking networks within nonprofit organizations by analyzing National Provider Identifier (NPI) distributions.

---

THE TOOL

NPI Calculator: https://github.com/Tonypost949/NPI---Non-Profiteers-Index

What it does:
- Audits nonprofit organizations for NPI clustering patterns
- Compares actual provider counts against control group benchmarks
- Identifies credential harvesting red flags (zero providers in behavioral health = fraud signal)
- Generates forensic reports suitable for federal grand juries
- Reveals connections to transnational trafficking networks

Who should use it:
- State Attorneys General (nonprofit fraud prosecution)
- Federal agencies (FBI, HHS-OIG, DOJ, FinCEN)
- IRS (Form 990 audit enforcement)
- Nonprofit watchdog organizations
- Journalists investigating organized fraud

---

CASE STUDY: ORANGE COUNTY FRAUD NETWORK ($6.6 BILLION EXPOSURE)

This tool was developed in response to a massive, documented $6.6 billion federal fraud network spanning Orange County, California. The NPI Calculator revealed the architectural pattern of this network.

Key Findings:

ChildNet (EIN 65-1149351) — The Credential Harvesting Hub
- $683 million in 5-year federal billing (Medicaid, Medicare, CalMedi-Cal)
- ZERO National Provider Identifiers in database (impossible for legitimate behavioral health nonprofit)
- Compared to control group: Sycamores (66 NPIs), Pressley Ridge (62), Aspiranet (45), Youth Villages (37), Olive Crest (29), Fred Finch (60)
- ChildNet's zero-NPI pattern = signature of credential harvesting fraud

Mercy House (EIN 33-0315864) — Self-Dealing & Trafficking
- Board members simultaneously own service provider companies billing same organization
- Johnny Bryant (ASL Electric) bills Mercy House for non-existent electrical work
- Credential harvesting for homeless trafficking victims
- Disabled residents poisoned by hexavalent chromium (49× legal limit) at shelter location (HBNC, 17641 Beach Blvd, Huntington Beach CA)

Federal Crime Pattern Identified:
- Tax fraud (false nonprofit status, fraudulent 990s)
- False Claims Act violations ($1.2B+ false Medicaid billing)
- Trafficking of vulnerable populations (homeless, disabled, children)
- Environmental crimes (hexavalent chromium Superfund violation)
- Record deletion (18 U.S.C. § 1519)
- Retaliation against whistleblowers (18 U.S.C. § 1513(e))

---

IMMEDIATE ACTION REQUIRED

HBNC Emergency (Human Lives at Stake)

Location: 17641 Beach Blvd, Huntington Beach CA
Crisis: 40+ disabled homeless residents actively being poisoned by hexavalent chromium at 49× the legal limit

body:
Hello Mr. Chen,


I hope this letter finds you well.


I am currently seeking an attorney. I have been guided by Government
assistance for a year and I am being told to seek an attorney now.


I am in the rental relief program and I was evicted at gun point after I
was told by Irvine City Officials my lockout was not going to happen. I was
intentionally lied to so that I would not know the dangerous and violent
situation was going to happen.  If my friend was not home with me, like me
and my young son usually were, I may not be here or my son.

My friends father is in the CIA. This “hit” on my life was ordered by my
billionaire landlord, Shea Properties.

There’s more, much more.


Here is a timeline list of what I have recorded and supplied the
Government. And I will also include a list of who I have been in contact
with.



My Background


I am a technical designer (CNC, 3D Print) for sanitation projects. I make
blueprints that allow the project to move forward.  I worked through Covid
and caught Covid bc I was working in essential services. People do not get
into their homes bc projects cannot finish without plans for the sanitation
being complete.  That was my job when Covid started.


Also all of the sales and marketing for the company were created and
executed by me. My sales systems produced over 500k a year in sales for the
company and I had to design all of it. I was barely paid and I couldn’t
stop working bc people needed to be in their homes during Covid. I created
custom systems and protocols to speed up the technical designs, which sped
up the project. And my sales system was running on its own, generating
revenue automatically , so I could focus on all the design work, when I was
laid off.


I am also an IHSS caretaker, it was my give back, I had to give that up.


I also was getting my son and his best friend  every other day from school
for the last 3 years, even through Covid. That big part of our life, I
worked so hard to achieve, was taken from us.


(2012)

I was the executive producer of Amerikidz

Magazine. I spearheaded distributing millions of copies profitably
throughout Orange County for years, and it was a free magazine.


(2008-2012)

I was a commodity broker and fintech designer.




Timeline of events/List


Jan 2021

I catch Covid , and so do the other employees and the boss


Feb 2021

I am hurting for funds from missed time with Covid, the dysfunction in the
shop affects everyone’s finances


I sign up for the rental RELEIF program bc of work becoming expensive due
to being late and other cost factors related to being sick with Covid
fallout


April 23rd

Shea employee runs onto my porch unexpectedly and very angry. He says my
payments and paperwork for RR were not correct and he announced to the
neighborhood I’m being evicted.

In front of my kid.


May 4th

My birthday

(I turned 38)

Woke up in my perfect ap

The following entities and their acting executive officers are named as
Defendants due to their direct roles in applying for, receiving, and
administering Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention (HHAP) funds, as
well as their fiduciary failure to allocate the legally mandated "Youth
Set-Aside" to the 30,000+ unhoused minors in their jurisdiction. The motive

the localized logistical costs of family sheltering and transportation.

for the county, the Board votes to accept and appropriate state grant
money. They are fiscally responsible for the county budget that absorbs
these funds.
* The County Executive Officer (CEO) of Orange County: The executive office
that oversees all county operations and budget implementations.
* The Orange County Office of Care Coordination (Director): The specific
county department tasked with acting as the administrative entity for the
Continuum of Care and managing the actual ledgers for the county's HHAP
grant allocations.

3. State Level Oversight and Distribution Agencies

Dear Federal Investigators, Nonprofit Advocates, Media, & Oversight Officials,

We are releasing a new open-source tool: the NPI Non-Profiteer Index Calculator — a free, auditable software platform designed to identify tax fraud, credential harvesting, and trafficking networks within nonprofit organizations by analyzing National Provider Identifier (NPI) distributions.

---

THE TOOL

NPI Calculator: https://github.com/Tonypost949/NPI---Non-Profiteers-Index

What it does:
- Audits nonprofit organizations for NPI clustering patterns
- Compares actual provider counts against control group benchmarks
- Identifies credential harvesting red flags (zero providers in behavioral health = fraud signal)
- Generates forensic reports suitable for federal grand juries
- Reveals connections to transnational trafficking networks

Who should use it:
- State Attorneys General (nonprofit fraud prosecution)
- Federal agencies (FBI, HHS-OIG, DOJ, FinCEN)
- IRS (Form 990 audit enforcement)
- Nonprofit watchdog organizations
- Journalists investigating organized fraud

---

CASE STUDY: ORANGE COUNTY FRAUD NETWORK ($6.6 BILLION EXPOSURE)

This tool was developed in response to a massive, documented $6.6 billion federal fraud network spanning Orange County, California. The NPI Calculator revealed the architectural pattern of this network.

Key Findings:

ChildNet (EIN 65-1149351) — The Credential Harvesting Hub
- $683 million in 5-year federal billing (Medicaid, Medicare, CalMedi-Cal)
- ZERO National Provider Identifiers in database (impossible for legitimate behavioral health nonprofit)
- Compared to control group: Sycamores (66 NPIs), Pressley Ridge (62), Aspiranet (45), Youth Villages (37), Olive Crest (29), Fred Finch (60)
- ChildNet's zero-NPI pattern = signature of credential harvesting fraud

Mercy House (EIN 33-0315864) — Self-Dealing & Trafficking
- Board members simultaneously own service provider companies billing same organization
- Johnny Bryant (ASL Electric) bills Mercy House for non-existent electrical work
- Credential harvesting for homeless trafficking victims
- Disabled residents poisoned by hexavalent chromium (49× legal limit) at shelter location (HBNC, 17641 Beach Blvd, Huntington Beach CA)

Federal Crime Pattern Identified:
- Tax fraud (false nonprofit status, fraudulent 990s)
- False Claims Act violations ($1.2B+ false Medicaid billing)
- Trafficking of vulnerable populations (homeless, disabled, children)
- Environmental crimes (hexavalent chromium Superfund violation)
- Record deletion (18 U.S.C. § 1519)
- Retaliation against whistleblowers (18 U.S.C. § 1513(e))

---

IMMEDIATE ACTION REQUIRED

HBNC Emergency (Human Lives at Stake)

Location: 17641 Beach Blvd, Huntington Beach CA
Crisis: 40+ disabled homeless residents actively being poisoned by hexavalent chromium at 49× the legal limit

Dear Federal Investigators, Nonprofit Advocates, Media, & Oversight Officials,

We are releasing a new open-source tool: the NPI Non-Profiteer Index Calculator — a free, auditable software platform designed to identify tax fraud, credential harvesting, and trafficking networks within nonprofit organizations by analyzing National Provider Identifier (NPI) distributions.

---

THE TOOL

NPI Calculator: https://github.com/Tonypost949/NPI---Non-Profiteers-Index

What it does:
- Audits nonprofit organizations for NPI clustering patterns
- Compares actual provider counts against control group benchmarks
- Identifies credential harvesting red flags (zero providers in behavioral health = fraud signal)
- Generates forensic reports suitable for federal grand juries
- Reveals connections to transnational trafficking networks

Who should use it:
- State Attorneys General (nonprofit fraud prosecution)
- Federal agencies (FBI, HHS-OIG, DOJ, FinCEN)
- IRS (Form 990 audit enforcement)
- Nonprofit watchdog organizations
- Journalists investigating organized fraud

---

CASE STUDY: ORANGE COUNTY FRAUD NETWORK ($6.6 BILLION EXPOSURE)

This tool was developed in response to a massive, documented $6.6 billion federal fraud network spanning Orange County, California. The NPI Calculator revealed the architectural pattern of this network.

ChildNet (EIN 65-1149351) — The Credential Harvesting Hub
- $683 million in 5-year federal billing (Medicaid, Medicare, CalMedi-Cal)

- ChildNet's zero-NPI pattern = signature of credential harvesting fraud

Mercy House (EIN 33-0315864) — Self-Dealing & Trafficking

- Johnny Bryant (ASL Electric) bills Mercy House for non-existent electrical work

New on Substack: Subscriber Perks, saved Notes, scheduled Chats, MCP,
 redesigned podcast player, and more
body:
View this post on the web at https://on.substack.com/p/new-on-substack-subscriber-perks

Whether you’re spending your Substack summer tinkering with your existing newsletter or podcast or launching your first one, we’re shipping features that make it easier to publish, customize, and distribute your work, and engage with your audience. We look forward to hearing what’s most useful and what you want more of. Here’s the latest.
Paid subscriber Perks
Subscriber Perks are a new feature that lets you give your paid audience something extra beyond traditional paywalled content, like discount codes, downloadable resources, or invites to live sessions. Perks you create will appear under the new “Perks” tab on your publication. It’s another way to thank the paid subscribers who support your work and encourage others to upgrade. This is available to publishers who have payments enabled.
Here are some perks publishers are already offering their paid subscribers:
Anna Eleri Hart ’s U.S. shopping guide
I LIKE NETWORKING ’s curated list of people to meet at SXSW London
Caroline Chambers ’s six-day meal plan
Learn more about subscriber perks in our Help Center [ https://substack.com/redirect/da1891bc-ea36-4991-be79-98f7d8e2c3f3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzNrMHZmIn0.wN8woLQ5vJyYy83fyWQx20gZ8aiG8YTyZQBwMBp12rY ].
Saved Notes
You can now save Notes on iOS and Android directly in the Substack app. Saved Notes live in your Substack profile. Just click on the ⋯ in the top right corner to access them.
This dedicated space for saved Notes within your profile is like your curated reading list, or as Ru Rao  put it [ https://substack.com/@ruarchv/note/c-275821748 ], the place to revisit a Note that’s an “absolute gem.”
Scheduled Chats
You can now schedule Chat threads just like you schedule Notes and posts. Scheduling chats is a great way to build community by connecting regularly with your audience between posts. Schedule a chat by going to the Chat tab, clicking the orange button to start a new Chat thread, and selecting “Schedule” in the thread settings
Polls
You can now post polls to Substack Notes. Polls are another way to continue the conversation with your audience by surfacing their opinions, preferences, and priorities. It’s just one click for them and can lead to a gold mine of ideas for you.
You can embed a poll in a Note or a post:
In a Note, click on the Poll icon in the bottom of the Note screen.
In a post, click “More” on the far right side of the text editor and select Poll from the dropdown menu.
Stephanie H. Murray , the writer of Family Stuff , recently restacked another publisher’s writing and polled her own audience to gauge their reaction to a parenting etiquette question. She received over 400 responses [ https://substack.com/@_/note/c-270125130 ].

subject: Jonathan Wilson’s World Cup Diary
body:
View this post on the web at https://on.substack.com/p/jonathan-wilsons-world-cup-diary

We caught up with veteran British soccer writer, podcaster, and historian of the game Jonathan Wilson  on the eve of his sixth World Cup final. Over the past six weeks, he’s been all over the map, filing from Mexico City, Guadalajara, Houston, and Boston for The Guardian, Bloomberg, the Paris Review, and more, while bringing literary dispatches and wry analysis to his own newsletter Wilson’s World (of football) [ https://substack.com/redirect/d10b9aec-f4b4-482c-b1ea-342a16746cc2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzNrMHZmIn0.wN8woLQ5vJyYy83fyWQx20gZ8aiG8YTyZQBwMBp12rY ]. We asked him to document the day he covered the Spain-France semifinal in Dallas and chatted with him about his Substack strategy, how he expanded his subscriber base by 40% over the course of the tournament, and his reckoning with the strange atmosphere at World Cup 2026.
Your sixth world cup! How many matches did you get to this time around?
Fifteen, I think. Maybe 16. I did three in Mexico City, three in Guadalajara, two in Monterrey, so that’s eight. I did four in Dallas, two in Houston, one in Boston. So 15 total!
I also loved your dispatches from the games you caught along the way: watching from hotel bars, or restaurant patios, or catching the Germany-Paraguay penalty shootout at an airport Chili’s.
I wasn’t even in it! I was outside the Chili’s. I was rushing through security to see the end, obviously had to make my flight, and I could see the screens. I was like, “Okay, I can just go over there and watch.” There were maybe about a dozen people there when I got there, and I got there at about 117 minutes. By the end of the penalties there were 60, 70, 80 people standing there. If you’d been selecting the most diverse group of people you could have found, you couldn’t have created a better one. There were a couple of security staff, a pilot, a couple of cleaners, a bloke in a Swiss shirt, loads of people with Mexican shirts, babies in pushchairs, old people in wheelchairs. People who clearly knew exactly what was going on, people who said, “I don’t understand this. What happens next?” It was the great World Cup moment of everybody coming together to watch this exciting denouement of the game.
How does that compare to being in the stadium?
In the stadium you get a much better feel for the game. It’s almost like a native speaker of a language. You have to start speaking a language before you’re 6 or 7 to really understand it. Football’s exactly the same. If you start going to games when you’re 4 or 5, you can smell what’s going to happen. You don’t know why, you can’t explain it, but it’s a very common thing for people who have been going from that age. That sense for a shift in emotional momentum—you get a much better feel for that in the stadium.

subject: Treasury Takes Largest Action Ever Targeting Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generacion
body:
Treasury Building Engraving

*U.S. Department of the Treasury*

Office of Public Affairs

*Press Release:            *July 23, 2026

*Contact:     *                Treasury Public Affairs, Press@treasury.gov

*Treasury Takes Largest Action Ever Targeting Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generacion*

"Sanctions Target CJNG’s Leadership, Drug Trafficking Cells, and Illicit Finance Networks Spread Across Mexico"

*WASHINGTON* – Today, in a sweeping action to confront narcoterrorism, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned over 50 Mexican individuals and entities linked to the terrorist group Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generacion (CJNG).  Today’s action disrupts a wide range of criminal activities benefitting CJNG across multiple Mexican states.  Among today’s targets is dual Mexican-U.S. national *Juan Carlos Gonzalez *(a.k.a. “Pelon”), who became the new leader of the cartel following the recent death of his stepfather, CJNG founder Ruben Oseguera Cervantes, a.k.a. “El Mencho.”  

“President Trump has made clear that terrorist cartels will be dismantled,” said *Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent*. “Today's action strikes Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generacion's leadership, financiers, and criminal networks, denying the cartel the resources it uses to traffic fentanyl, terrorize communities, and threaten American lives.”

CJNG, which is based in Mexico but active globally, is a violent cartel and Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) that is responsible for a significant proportion of fentanyl and other deadly drugs trafficked into the United States.  CJNG employs sophisticated money laundering methodologies and alternative revenue streams, such as fuel theft and smuggling and timeshare fraud.  Today’s action was taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 14059, which targets the international proliferation of illicit drugs and their means of production, and pursuant to E.O. 13224, as amended, which targets terrorists and their supporters."  "

In keeping with President Trump’s pledge to eliminate cartels, OFAC has prioritized targeting these and other criminal groups that threaten the welfare of Americans in close coordination with the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF), taking nearly 30 actions against 250 individuals and entities.  OFAC uses a network-based approach to simultaneously disrupt as many different facets of the cartels as possible, from their leadership and key organizational nodes to facilitators and enablers, such as corrupt officials, complicit family members, and ostensibly legitimate front persons.

body: Email from California Commission on Asian & Pacific Islander American Affairs Our Biggest Moments and Statewide Engagement   2026 Summer Newsletter A Message from Commission Chair Jason Paguio Dear Friends and Community Members, As we reflect on the first half of 2026, we are grateful for the collective leadership, partnership, and community engagement that continue to guide the work of the California Commission on Asian and Pacific Islander American Affairs. Across the State Capitol, campuses, cultural celebrations, policy briefings, and community gatherings, CAPIAA has remained focused on ensuring that Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities are seen, heard, and represented in the decisions shaping California. This year has shown what is possible when commissioners, policymakers, advocates, educators, and community partners work together around a shared commitment to equity and representation. CAPIAA has continued advancing legislative and policy priorities focused on AANHPI-serving institutions, student representation, data equity, and sustained investment in community safety. We also welcomed Commissioners Manju Kulkarni and Zain Yahya, whose experience in civil rights, community advocacy, business, and public policy further strengthens the Commission’s leadership and statewide perspective. One of this year’s most significant milestones was advocating to extend California’s $30 million investment in the Stop the Hate Program. This funding will empower trusted organizations across the state to expand culturally responsive services, strengthen rapid-response networks, support those impacted by hate, and advance prevention efforts. At the same time, our continued work around co-sponsoring AB 2017, AB 2374, ACA 18, and AB 1878 reflects CAPIAA’s commitment to advancing policies rooted in visibility, participation, accountability, and investment. Our work has also been shaped by opportunities to listen and learn directly from communities. Through the Afghan Community Listening Session, advocacy days, policy briefings, educational convenings, and regional gatherings, we heard from residents, students, educators, advocates, and organizational leaders whose perspectives will continue to inform CAPIAA’s priorities. The release of the State of Higher Education for AANHPI Californians Report in partnership with the Campaign for College Opportunity further underscored the importance of disaggregated data, culturally responsive support, and equitable pathways that reflect the full diversity of AANHPI student experiences. As we look ahead to the second half of the year, CAPIAA remains committed to creating more opportunities for Californians to participate in shaping our work. We look forward to our upcoming Filipino Community Listening Session, the Annual Report Youth Cover Design Contest, Fall Internship Cohort, and continued engagement with partners across the state.
